The proposal was brought to the floor outside the planned order of proceedings on Friday. Speaker Tomio Okamura of the SPD limited debate and scheduled the vote for 4:36 a.m. (0336 GMT) on Saturday. The coalition's majority then voted to send the bill to committees for further discussion. SUNDAY PROTEST PLANNED Hundreds of protesters gathered outside parliament, with some remaining overnight. Local media reported that several people unsuccessfully tried to enter the building. Critics say the changes would weaken the broadcasters and make them more vulnerable to political pressure. Czech Television is the country's most-watched broadcaster across major age groups, while public media are among the most trusted news sources in the country, according to a 2025 Reuters Institute survey. The proposal would cut funding for Czech Television and Czech Radio by about 15%, possibly as early as next year, and keep nominal funding unchanged for several years. "There is no war for independent media," Babis said on Facebook late on Friday. "There is no fight for democracy and no nationalisation of media is being prepared." The proposal and its fast-track treatment drew criticism from the broadcasters, international journalism groups and institutions including universities and the Catholic Church. "The bill goes against the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA), which requires adequate, stable and predictable funding for public service media," the European Federation of Journalists said in a statement. Journalists and other employees at the broadcasters announced a strike for November 3, while a civic group called a public protest for Sunday. ($1 = 21.6880 Czech crowns)

item.title: Le dirigeant nord-coréen Kim Jong Un en visite en Chine
item.description: Le dirigeant de la Corée du Nord Kim Jong Un s'est rendu samedi en Chine en empruntant un pont tout juste ouvert entre les deux pays, a-t-on appris d'un responsable gouvernemental sud-coréen.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Le dirigeant de la Corée du Nord Kim Jong Un s'est rendu samedi en Chine en empruntant un pont tout juste ouvert entre les deux pays, a-t-on appris d'un responsable gouvernemental sud-coréen. Kim est arrivé dans la ville chinoise de Dandong en empruntant un pont au-dessus du fleuve Yalu, a ajouté ce responsable s'exprimant sous le sceau de l'anonymat. Il a été accueilli dans cette ville frontalière par le Premier ministre chinois, Li Qiang, a rapporté l'agence sud-coréenne Yonhap. On ignore s'il rencontrera le président chinois Xi Jinping. Le ministère chinois des Affaires étrangères n'a pas répondu dans l'immédiat à une demande de commentaire. Long de trois kilomètres, le Nouveau Pont du fleuve Yalu été inauguré ce mois-ci avec un long retard sur le calendrier initial. Il constitue désormais la plus importante liaison terrestre entre la Corée du Nord et la Chine. Son ouverture doit permettre de relancer les relations commerciales entre les deux pays après des années de perturbations dues à des tensions diplomatiques et aux effets de la pandémie de COVID-19. Elle illustre aussi le réchauffement en cours entre la Chine et la Corée du Nord, dont les dirigeants ont participé à deux sommets lors des 13 derniers mois.

item.title: Allemagne-Le "nid d'aigle" des nazis en Bavière incendié
item.description: Le "nid d'aigle", ancienne résidence des dignitaires du régime nazi dans les montagnes bavaroises du sud de l'Allemagne, a pris feu vendredi soir et un suspect a été arrêté, a annoncé la police allemande.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Le "nid d'aigle", ancienne résidence des dignitaires du régime nazi dans les montagnes bavaroises du sud de l'Allemagne, a pris feu vendredi soir et un suspect a été arrêté, a annoncé la police allemande. Environ 200 pompiers ont été déployés pour lutter contre l'incendie ravageant le bâtiment, le Kehlsteinhaus, près de Berchtesgaden. La police a dit avoir arrêté un suspect près des lieux du sinistre. Aucune piste n'a été évoquée concernant un éventuel mobile. Construite en 1938 en tant que lieu de retraite pour les dignitaires nazis et leurs invités, cette bâtisse érigée au milieu des reliefs des Alpes est distincte de la résidence d'été d'Adolf Hitler, située à proximité et baptisée le Berghof. Désormais propriété du Land de Bavière, le Kehlsteinhaus a été classé monument historique après la Seconde Guerre mondiale.

The aviation accident on Friday involved two SF-260 aircraft during a training flight at the Fernando Air Base in Batangas province, the Philippine Air Force said in a statement Local media has reported the two planes collided in midair The aircraft crashed within the grounds of the air base but there were no other casualties The Air Force has temporarily grounded its fleet of SF-260 trainer planes pending an investigation into the cause of the accident In May, two pilots were killed when an SF-260 trainer aircraft crashed in a mountainous area in northern Philippines, while another SF-260 TP Marchetti [USN:L4N34A68W TEXT:"crashed"] during a 2023 training flight, also killing two pilots The military used SF-260 aircraft during months of air strikes on southern [USN:KBN1CS0DM TEXT:"Marawi City"] after militants loyal to Islamic State seized the area in 2017

item.title: France's luxury stores board up windows ahead of fresh protests
item.description: Some decided staying open was too risky after last week's unrest.
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Parodi
item.content:encoded: Luxury boutiques in France boarded up their normally glitzy shopfronts and hired private security ahead of [USN:L5N46A00Q TEXT:"fresh protests"] on Saturday, with some planning to stay closed after rioters looted stores across the country last weekend. France, the world's most visited country, attracts large numbers of overseas shoppers seeking Chanel handbags and Hermes scarves, an important source of revenue for luxury brands grappling with slowing demand. But some decided staying open was too risky after [USN:L1N46608H TEXT:"last week's unrest"], when rioters smashed and looted hundreds of shops in Paris, Marseille and Bordeaux. A Rolex retailer and a De Beers store near Paris' Place Vendome will remain closed on Saturday, staff said, while managers at stores including Richemont-owned (CFR.S) IWC said they would decide whether to close early depending on the scale of the protests. Signs on the heavily boarded-up windows of Adidas (ADSGn.DE) and Boss (BOSSn.DE) stores on the Champs Elysees informed customers they would be closed, while employees at Swatch Group (UHR.S) stores said they would shut early. A Lacoste store was entirely covered by metal cages after suffering what a staff member described as "enormous" damage last week. A café owned by the brand was completely boarded up. Groups including France's main student union, UNEF, and the Yellow Vest movement, which emerged as a powerful anti-establishment force in 2018, plan to march through central Paris later on Saturday to protest against high living costs and cuts to public services. Near the Arc de Triomphe, tourists photographed boarded-up stores and restaurants as they tried to take selfies beneath the landmark before the protests begin. Hotel staff said they were advising worried guests on the protest route and areas to avoid, leaving major tourist streets largely empty despite a heavy police and private security presence. NOT IN THE MOOD Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said on Friday that 70,000 police officers, backed by specialist units, would be deployed to prevent a repeat of last week's violence. But staff at LVMH brands Louis Vuitton, Dior and Bulgari said they were taking no chances and security at their stores near Place Vendome had been increased. The group had also deployed additional private security to patrol high-end shopping districts, several employees said. Nearby department store Printemps has also increased its security staff, carried out repairs and reinforced shop windows and entrances, a spokesperson said. Hermes finance chief Eric du Halgouet said this week the company had [USN:S8N3Z600A TEXT:"strengthened security"] at its French stores, adding it was too early to assess the impact of recent events on business. The image-conscious industry can ill afford further negative publicity. Consumer sentiment is gloomy worldwide and tourism is slowing as a result of the Iran war , contributing to disappointing quarterly results this month from [USN:L6N45Y0VL TEXT:"LVMH"] (LVMH.PA) , [USN:L6N46816C TEXT:"Hermes"] (HRMS.PA) and [USN:L6N4680E3 TEXT:"Kering"] (PRTP.PA) . Lidiya Shevchenko, a sales assistant at a Graziella Braccialini store, said she doubted many people would be looking to visit stores anyway during the protests. "I suppose the mood is just as important when it comes to shopping," Shevchenko said. One tourist already thinking twice is Cambodian Jerry Lay, who purchased several items from Louis Vuitton on the Champs-Élysées earlier this week. "We do enjoy shopping in France, but after experiencing the protest (last Saturday), I'd say it's 50/50 whether I would consider coming back next time," Lay said.

item.title: Jordan tightens security after deadly church attack kills eight
item.description: Security was stepped up at malls, foreign embassies and other locations across Jordan, the US embassy in Amman said on Saturday, as authorities searched for gunmen who killed eight people and wounded 40 in a church attack.
item.dc:creator: Abdelhadi Ramahi
item.content:encoded: Security was stepped up at malls, foreign embassies and other locations across Jordan, the US embassy in Amman said on Saturday, as authorities searched for gunmen who killed eight people and wounded 40 in a church attack. The assailants fired for several minutes in broad daylight [USN:L6N46A02E TEXT:"during a funeral"] at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate on Friday, in what Jordanian authorities described as an act of extremist terrorism. There was no immediate claim of responsibility. Such attacks are rare in Jordan, although authorities in the US-allied kingdom say they have repeatedly foiled plots by Islamist militants in recent years. Bahjat al-Rushda, mayor of Shihan village in Karak, joined a long list of officials condemning what he called a "wicked" attack. "God willing, this country will remain secure," he said. Authorities said they were still searching for the attackers, adding it was too early to determine whether they had links to known groups inside or outside Jordan. "A massacre, a massacre in every sense of the word," said Tarek Ammarin at a hospital where the wounded were being treated. A relative of Ammarin's was injured in the attack. Reuters video footage showed police patrolling on Saturday outside the Hamoud church, about 120 km (75 miles) southwest of the capital Amman. "This is a result of a terrorist ideology and blind extremism and we will not allow society to go down this path," Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said in a post on X. Jordan's King Abdullah, a US partner in the fight against militant Islamist groups, visited Karak hours after the attack and said the perpetrators would be punished "with an iron fist". Christians make up a minority of Jordan's population. The country is home to several biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world. Jordan has been among the US allies in the Middle East to be hit by Iranian attacks this year after the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February.

item.title: North Korea's Kim crosses new bridge into China as trade ties warm
item.description: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday, Xinhua reported, crossing a newly opened bridge in a symbolic move seen as highlighting Beijing and Pyongyang's push to expand trade ties.
item.dc:creator: Joyce Lee, Eduardo Baptista
item.content:encoded: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday, Xinhua reported, crossing a newly opened bridge in a symbolic move seen as highlighting Beijing and Pyongyang's push to expand trade ties. Kim was accompanied during his visit by China's fourth-highest-ranked official Wang Huning, who conveyed greetings from President Xi Jinping, the official Xinhua news agency said. Kim arrived in Dandong via the [USN:L6N46004I TEXT:"New Yalu River Bridge"] connecting North Korea and China , a South Korean government official said on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak publicly. The new bridge is expected to help move heavy equipment, raw materials and energy products that North Korea needs for development. Its official opening this month is the latest sign of warming ties between Beijing and Pyongyang, after two summits between their leaders in the past 13 months. China, which fought alongside North Korea in the 1950-1953 Korean War, remains Pyongyang's main economic and diplomatic backer and accounts for most of its official trade. CHINESE TV SHOWS KIM WALKING ON BRIDGE But North Korea's deepening military ties with Russia since Moscow's 2022 invasion of Ukraine have led analysts to question whether Pyongyang is becoming less reliant on Beijing. Kim's trip nevertheless points to a renewed push by China and North Korea to bolster their economic relationship. South Korea's Yonhap news agency had earlier reported that Kim was expected to return to North Korea after Saturday's visit. Footage from Chinese state broadcaster CCTV showed Kim walking on the bridge, lined by people waving flags, towards North Korea. Xinhua said Wang accompanied Kim to a Korean War memorial in Dandong, where the North Korean leader paid tribute to Chinese People's Volunteer Army soldiers who fought alongside North Korea during the three-year conflict. Kim also toured a Dandong [USN:RTV844HDK TEXT:"automobile factory"], it said. NEW YALU RIVER BRIDGE BOOSTS BILATERAL TIES China and North Korea opened the 3 km (2 mile) New Yalu River Bridge, their most significant [USN:L1N46103M TEXT:"land border crossing"], this month after a long delay, aiming to rejuvenate trade and commerce after years of strained ties and pandemic-related disruptions. "Kim has given his imprimatur to bilateral trade by crossing the New Yalu River Bridge to enter China," said Christopher Green, a Korea specialist at Leiden University in the Netherlands, saying the delayed opening had shown how dysfunctional the relationship had become. During a meeting on Saturday, Wang told Kim that China was ready to use the bridge's opening to expand personnel exchanges and economic and trade cooperation, Xinhua said. A visit by Kim now is consistent with the current phase of closer economic ties and more frequent high-level exchanges between China and North Korea, said Lu Chao, an expert in China-North Korea relations at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, a Chinese government think-tank in Shenyang. "The opening of the bridge has resolved a major bottleneck in China-North Korea trade logistics," Lu said. "With the logistics constraint eased, bilateral trade is likely to increase further." TRUMP WAITS FOR KIM TO ENGAGE Kim's last known visit to China was in September 2025, to attend the 80th Victory Day celebrations in Beijing, when he held a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Xi made a [USN:L1N42G106 TEXT:"state visit"] to North Korea in June. US President Donald Trump has been eager to jump-start talks with North Korea, but US and South Korean officials see [USN:L1N4690EW TEXT:"fading chances"] of him meeting Kim this year, Reuters reported on Friday. China hosts a summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum next month in Shenzhen, which Trump is expected to attend.

item.title: How Trump's energy dominance turned into hubris
item.description: When Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, “energy dominance” was the bedrock of his economic and foreign policy plans. But an unpopular war with Iran and soaring household fuel costs have now made energy policy a major liability for the US president heading into next month’s midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: Ron Bousso
item.content:encoded: When Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, [USN:L1N3Q1127 TEXT:"“energy dominance”"] was the bedrock of his economic and foreign policy plans. But an unpopular war with Iran and soaring household fuel costs have now made energy policy a major liability for the US president heading into next month’s midterm elections . Ironically, it was the US position as the world's top oil and gas producer, perhaps more than anything else, that enabled Trump to pursue foreign policy goals that may turn out to be the costliest of his political career. In the first two years of Trump’s second term, vast US oil and gas resources emboldened Washington abroad, strengthened its hand in trade disputes and underpinned a broader effort to restore US geopolitical dominance. Yet the Iran war exposed the central weakness in that vision: dominating energy production does not mean controlling energy prices. What began as a pursuit of US energy independence evolved into a doctrine of energy dominance. That is now looking like energy hubris. UNLEASHING AMERICAN ENERGY The foundations of Trump’s strategy were laid long before his return to office last year. The development of cost-effective techniques to tap the country's onshore shale basins transformed the US into the world’s largest producer of natural gas in 2009 and petroleum in 2018. By 2022, it was the leading exporter of liquefied natural gas, giving Washington unprecedented influence over global energy markets. US crude production rose from around 5.5 million barrels per day in 2010 to nearly 14 million bpd today, around a fifth of global supplies, while the country also accounts for more than a quarter of global LNG exports. No single nation has ever occupied such a commanding position in the global energy system. Trump sought to turn that advantage into a governing doctrine. On his first day back in office, he declared a national energy emergency and ordered the government to [USN:S0N3NI004 TEXT:"“unleash American energy”"], prioritising oil, gas, coal and nuclear power while sidelining renewables. Within weeks, he made “energy dominance” official US policy, establishing the National Energy Dominance Council and reviving his familiar “drill, baby, drill” slogan as the purported cure for elevated inflation and economic anxiety. In an October 2025 proclamation, Trump summed up the philosophy as “maximum production, maximum prosperity, and maximum power”. ENERGY POLICY IS FOREIGN POLICY This doctrine extended far beyond domestic energy policy. The administration’s national security strategy, published last December, explicitly linked US influence in the Western Hemisphere to energy dominance, drawing on the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine that sought to oppose European political intervention in the region. In a little over a year, the administration wielded US oil and LNG exports in trade negotiations, promoted energy deals as part of efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war , and highlighted Greenland’s resource wealth in a push for greater influence over the [USN:L6N45E05Y TEXT:"Arctic territory"]. The high-water mark for Trump’s energy doctrine arguably came early this year after [USN:L6N3Y407K TEXT:"Washington removed Venezuelan President"] Nicolas Maduro in a swift military operation. The US subsequently [USN:L1N3ZM1KL TEXT:"took control"] of Venezuelan oil exports and revenues, forced through changes to the country’s hydrocarbons legislation that displaced Chinese companies, and secured an unprecedented agreement granting it access to a fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves. By February, Trump’s vision of building an economy and foreign policy around abundant fossil fuel resources appeared to be taking root. The US possessed not only more energy than any rival, but also the ability to use that abundance to shape trade, diplomacy and security. Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran in late February put that doctrine to the test. THE IRAN QUAGMIRE The president initially claimed that the joint campaign with Israel against Iran would last only a few weeks. He also repeatedly indicated that vast US oil and gas resources, together with newfound access to Venezuela’s oil wealth, would shield the economy from any resulting spike in energy costs, which he also suggested would be brief. Those assumptions have not aged well. The war launched on February 28 led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global energy supplies used to flow, triggering one of the largest energy disruptions in modern history. Middle Eastern producers cut output and rerouted exports where possible, while major importers across Asia reduced consumption. This caused oil prices to nearly double in the first two months of the conflict, with global benchmark Brent crude peaking at $118 a barrel in March. That was well below the record [USN:L03220220 TEXT:"$145 reached in 2008"], when Iran-related geopolitical tensions, surging Chinese demand and a weakening US dollar drove prices higher. It was also far less than many had feared, largely thanks to reduced Chinese oil imports, ample crude stocks and the surprising adaptability of global markets. But it still represented a severe shock. Moreover, the risk premium from the Iran war is becoming entrenched. Even though crude flows from the Middle East have mostly recovered, Brent is trading around $110. The conflict has also spread across the Middle East, pulling in most of Washington's Gulf allies, most notably the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, which have suffered multiple deadly attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis. This has upended the market’s confidence in the security of Middle Eastern crude, unravelled longstanding supply routes and sent [USN:L6N45R160 TEXT:"shipping prices"] skyrocketing. Trump wanted to put his stamp on global energy markets, but this was clearly not what he had in mind. PAIN AT THE PUMP In one respect, the 2026 energy shock has vindicated Trump’s strategy. The war cemented the US position as the world’s top supplier of crude, refined fuels and LNG, delivering enormous profits to domestic producers and exporters and allowing the US to expand its position in the global market. Energy independence certainly offered US consumers some protection against the energy shock, particularly compared with Asian economies, where prices and demand destruction were much more extreme this year. But that protection has been far from ironclad. US gasoline prices at the pump climbed above $4.60 a gallon in May, the highest level since 2022, while [USN:L1N45211Q TEXT:"diesel"] surged to a record $6.50 a gallon in September as global refining capacity was squeezed. Those increases rapidly became a political problem for the White House as cost-of-living concerns moved to the forefront of the campaign ahead of the midterms on November 3. The administration sought to contain the fuel-price spike by pulling almost every available lever, including [USN:L6N44M0V8 TEXT:"easing biofuel blending mandates"] and, most controversially, reaching a [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"diesel supply agreement"] with Russian President Vladimir Putin. This dynamic underscores the difference between commanding supply and controlling prices. Oil, LNG and refined fuels are internationally traded commodities. US producers sell them at prices shaped by global supply and demand. They don’t typically reserve cheap energy for American households. While Trump briefly floated the idea of a [USN:L6N45E0T3 TEXT:"diesel export ban"], officials ultimately rejected it. Even though a ban might have brought down domestic prices initially, it would likely have resulted in higher fuel prices over the medium term due to global market dynamics. ‘ENERGY SECURITY IS NATIONAL SECURITY’ The administration’s assertion last October that “energy security is national security” appears more relevant than ever. The Iran war has shown that cheap and reliable energy is essential for economic growth, whether it powers heavy industry or the data centres underpinning the artificial intelligence race. But the conflict has also changed the meaning of energy security. For countries dependent on imports, particularly [USN:L6N3ZY18D TEXT:"many in Asia"], the shock has revealed the risks of relying heavily on distant suppliers, vulnerable shipping routes and a concentrated global refining system. Their response is likely to be broader diversification: securing more suppliers, expanding domestic fossil fuel production where possible, accelerating renewable power and shifting more transport towards electricity. That will not kick the US off its lofty energy perch, but it will likely weaken the allure of oil and gas for many countries over the coming years. Trump likely felt emboldened to embark on the Iran war — something his predecessors had baulked at — precisely because US energy independence made a Middle East adventure seem less risky than it had when the US was heavily reliant on Gulf oil and gas. But the conflict has, perhaps permanently, undermined Trump’s promise that energy dominance would guarantee low prices and economic security at home. Hubris can be a dangerous thing. item.title: Mumbai Indians promote Pollard to head coach, replacing Jayawardene
item.description: Mumbai Indians have appointed Kieron Pollard as head coach for the 2027 season in place of Mahela Jayawardene, the Indian Premier League team said on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Mumbai Indians have appointed Kieron Pollard as head coach for the 2027 season in place of Mahela Jayawardene, the Indian Premier League team said on Saturday. Pollard, who helped the West Indies win the Twenty20 World Cup in 2012 and won five IPL titles with the Mumbai Indians between 2013 and 2020, served as the team's batting coach under Jayawardene before the [USN:L4N46300R TEXT:"Sri Lankan's departure"] last week. Mumbai Indians are the joint most-successful side in IPL history, with five titles, but have struggled since their last victory, finishing outside the playoffs in four of the past six seasons. "Having experienced this journey as a player and then as a coach, I understand what Mumbai Indians stands for and the responsibility that comes with representing the Blue and Gold," the 39-year-old said in a statement. "I look forward to working closely with the players and support staff, building on the team's legacy, helping our talent grow and giving the (fans) many more reasons to celebrate."

item.title: Último debate entre Flávio e Lula reedita troca de acusações e avança pouco em propostas
item.description: A dois dias do segundo turno da eleição presidencial, o debate entre os dois candidatos -- o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) -- na TV Globo foi palco de mais um round de trocas de acusações e avançou um pouco em relação à exposição de planos de governo.
item.dc:creator: Maria Marcello
item.content:encoded: A dois dias do segundo turno da eleição presidencial, o debate entre os dois candidatos -- o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) -- na TV Globo foi palco de mais um round de trocas de acusações e avançou um pouco em relação à exposição de planos de governo. Os candidatos foram para o debate com estratégias específicas de olho no eleitor indeciso. Flávio decidiu focar no custo de vida e prometeu manter programas sociais. Lula chamou a atenção para a defesa da democracia e lembrou que foram os governos petistas que criaram e reforçaram os programas sociais em vigor. "Em quatro anos de governo, você consegue comprar mais ou menos com o seu salário?", questionou Flávio. "Está difícil comprar. Quando você consegue comprar, você está levando menos para a sua casa, esse é o legado do atual governo", disse Flávio. Já Lula, não só defendeu a democracia como acusou o adversário de "miliciano". "Eu sou um homem que tenho biografia, tenho história", disse o presidente. "Eu queria, primeiro agradecer... e pedir o voto de vocês no domingo porque ou a gente mantém a democracia funcionando ou a gente vai ter um miliciano governando esse país dentro do Palácio do Planalto", disse Lula, em menção a Flávio que rendeu um direito de resposta ao senador. Flávio negou envolvimento com milícia na sequência -- "isso é coisa da sua cabeça" -- e prometeu classificar as milícias como narcoterroristas. A organização do debate chegou a impor regras sobre a circulação dos candidatos, de forma a evitar desgastes ocorridos no debate de domingo na TV Band. Veículos e entidades paralelamente fizeram o acompanhamento do debate para checagem de fatos. Mas ainda assim, houve uma reedição de trocas de acusações e era perceptível o clima de Fla-Flu na plateia, que em alguns momentos chegou a se manifestar. Lula questionou Flávio sobre posicionamentos públicos do senador contrários a programas sociais e chegou a perguntar ao senador por que se referiu ao Bolsa-Família como "Bolsa-Farelo". Flávio, por sua vez, apontou a gestão petista dos gastos públicos como responsável pelos juros altos, que resvalam no poder de compra da população. No quesito juros, aliás, Lula lembrou que foi no governo de Jair Bolsonaro, pai de Flávio, que foi aprovada a autonomia do Banco Central, entidade responsável pela definição da taxa básica de juros do país. Os candidatos também conseguiram emplacar argumentos e frases com forte apelo, principalmente para os cortes e edições de trechos a serem usados nas redes sociais nessas últimas horas antes da abertura das urnas eleitorais. Em resposta a Flávio, que referiu-se ao presidente como "nove dedos", Lula lembrou que perdeu o dedo em um acidente de trabalho. "Se tem alguém aqui nesse púlpito que sabe o que é o mundo do trabalho sou eu. Se tem alguém que perdeu o dedo com 17 anos fui eu", disse Lula, provocando reações da plateia. "Milhões de trabalhadores se acidentam por irresponsabilidade patronal, que obriga a gente a trabalhar em jornada que a gente tem que trabalhar. Eu era menor e trabalhava à noite, porque ou trabalhava ou não comia e não vou aceitar que um granfino, com uma prática política muito duvidosa, venha me chamar de nove dedos." Após a dura declaração do presidente, Flávio se desculpou, dizendo que não tinha intenção de ser ofensivo. O senador, por outro lado, buscou se apresentar como o candidato da mudança, da novidade. "Nem parece que ele é o atual presidente da República... Ele parece que parou no tempo. Infelizmente o atual presidente da República, as ideias que ele tinha -- que eram boas lá atrás --... hoje não funcionam mais", afirmou. Os dois também cometeram deslizes no decorrer do debate. Lula volta e meia se perdia nas regras e precisava ser lembrado pelo moderador que ainda tinha tempo para desenvolver sua fala. Já Flávio -- questionado por Lula sobre sua escolha em atuar na defesa de um policial acusado de matar uma criança de 5 anos em Niterói, no Rio de Janeiro -- cometeu um equívoco. Na intenção de prestar solidariedade à mãe da menina, que estava na plateia, se confundiu ao chamá-la pelo nome da criança morta. Em outro momento, o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro voltou a ser citado. Lula cobrou Flávio sobre o dinheiro que pediu ao banqueiro -- o senador reafirmou que era para o financiamento de um filme sobre seu pai, o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro. O senador, por sua vez, acusou Lula de receber um uísque do banqueiro de presente. Houve até mesmo uma renovação do desafio de Lula para que os dois abram suas contas bancárias e provem que não são corruptos. Flávio Bolsonaro é alvo de dois inquéritos no STF: um que apura suspeitas relacionadas exatamente ao financiamento do filme "Dark Horse" e outro sobre suspeita de lavagem de dinheiro envolvendo o advogado Willer Tomaz. Mas se Lula não é alvo de investigação criminal conhecida atualmente, Flávio voltou a se concentrar em seu filho, conhecido como Lulinha, que é investigado pela Polícia Federal sobre suposto tráfico de influência. Na segunda metade do debate, quando os ataques e acusações de ambos os candidatos se intensificaram, a plateia começou a se manifestar e a reagir a respostas dos presidenciáveis. O clima, no entanto, foi mais ameno que no debate do último domingo.

item.title: Atlético de San Luis gana de visita al Atlante en el torneo mexicano de fútbol
item.description: Atlético de San Luis sacó el viernes un triunfo de su visita al Atlante por 1-0 en la decimocuarta jornada del torneo Apertura del fútbol mexicano.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Atlético de San Luis sacó el viernes un triunfo de su visita al Atlante por 1-0 en la decimocuarta jornada del torneo Apertura del fútbol mexicano. Con su quinto triunfo, Atlético de San Luis llegó a 19 puntos para ubicarse en el décimo lugar general, cerca de la zona que da acceso a la postemporada. Los clubes que ocupan los primeros ocho lugares de la tabla general al final de las 17 jornadas de la temporada regular clasifican a dicha instancia. En el partido disputado en el estadio Azteca de la Ciudad de México, Atlético de San Luis se puso en ventaja a los 59 minutos por conducto de Benjamín Galdames, quien metió el balón por el ángulo izquierdo con un disparo desde el vértice del área. En el transcurso del encuentro, ambos clubes tuvieron opciones de anotar, pero las atinadas intervenciones de los porteros evitaron que se concretaran. Atlante tuvo la oportunidad más clara de empatar en tiempo de reposición con un tiro penal, pero el portero Gibran Lajud tapó el disparo del paraguayo Walter Clar, quien en el contraremate estrelló el balón en el travesaño a los 94 minutos. En el otro partido que se jugó el viernes, Necaxa y Bravos de Ciudad Juárez empataron 1-1. Para Necaxa anotó Owen González y para Bravos de Ciudad Juárez lo hizo Luca Martínez. El sábado, León jugará ante Toluca, Guadalajara visitará a Monterrey y Pumas UNAM enfrentará a Tigres UANL. El domingo, Atlas será local ante Puebla, el actual campeón Cruz Azul visitará a Querétaro, el líder América jugará ante Pachuca y Tijuana será rival de Santos Laguna.

item.title: Late 17-0 surge carries Grizzlies to comeback win over Warriors
item.description: Ty Jerome scored a game-high 28 points and the Memphis Grizzlies used a 17-0 fourth-quarter spurt to rally for a 111-108 victory over the Golden State Warriors in San Francisco on Friday.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Ty Jerome scored a game-high 28 points and the Memphis Grizzlies used a 17-0 fourth-quarter spurt to rally for a 111-108 victory over the Golden State Warriors in San Francisco on Friday. Rookie Cameron Boozer added 25 points, 13 rebounds and six assists for Memphis, which won its second straight game to begin the season. Jaylen Wells scored 17 and Cam Spencer chipped in 11 for the Grizzlies, who outscored Golden State 27-18 in the fourth quarter. Stephen Curry's 24 points led the Warriors, while Brandin Podziemski and rookie Yaxel Lendeborg contributed 18 points apiece. In his second career game, Lendeborg also tallied 13 rebounds and six assists. Graham Ike and De'Anthony Melton both scored 10 points for Golden State, which has dropped its first two games of the year for the first time since 2020-21. After trailing by four at halftime, Golden State took its first lead of the third quarter on Podziemski's 3-pointer with 2:09 left to put the Warriors ahead 86-84. Golden State finished the third on an 11-0 run and held a 90-84 advantage entering the final quarter. Spencer hit a triple to cut Memphis' deficit to three with 6:54 left before Melton and Lendeborg made back-to-back treys and Podziemski sank a driving layup to extend Golden State's lead to 103-92. Melton drilled another triple to make it a 12-point game with 3:47 to go, but the Grizzlies answered with 17 straight points, including Boozer's turnaround jumper to give the visitors a 108-106 lead with 20.1 seconds left. Draymond Green was then whistled for an offensive foul, leading to a technical foul on Warriors coach Steve Kerr with 12.8 seconds remaining. Jerome made the technical foul shot and hit a layup to give Memphis a 111-106 lead. Lendeborg rebounded a Melton miss and was fouled with a half-second remaining. He made both foul shots to cut the deficit to three. The Grizzlies then ran out the clock on the ensuing possession to ice the comeback win. Podziemski sank each of his four first-quarter field-goal attempts, including a buzzer-beating runner, to help the Warriors take a 34-33 lead into the second quarter. Trailing by a point, Memphis rattled off a 16-2 run and grabbed a 54-41 lead on Spencer's 3-pointer with 4:42 remaining in the first half. A 10-0 Golden State run, stamped with Gui Santos' free throws, pulled the Warriors within a point. Jerami Grant finished the opening half with a three-point play to give the Grizzlies a 60-56 advantage at the break. --Field Level Media

item.title: Trump foreign policy hits voters in the pocketbook, imperiling Republicans in midterms
item.description: Foreign policy is rarely the deciding factor in US midterm elections. But this time, Trump’s approach to world affairs has itself become a pocketbook issue.
item.dc:creator: Matt Spetalnick
item.content:encoded: Foreign policy is rarely the deciding factor in US midterm elections, when economic considerations usually drive voters’ choices. But this time, with Donald Trump’s war against Iran and his sweeping tariff campaign pushing up costs for Americans, a president’s approach to world affairs has itself become a pocketbook issue. As the November 3 elections approach, there are growing signs that voters are drawing that connection directly, creating a major liability for Trump and his fellow Republicans and imperiling their control of Congress. Those include a Reuters/Ipsos poll earlier this month showing some 78% of Americans [USN:L6N45T0W3 TEXT:"blame Trump's policies"] for rising prices that are outpacing their earnings. Not since 2006, when President George W. Bush’s Republicans lost both legislative chambers while he was mired in the unpopular Iraq war, has a US leader’s handling of international events appeared so central to shaping the midterms outcome. The political backlash for Trump could be even bigger, with opinion polls showing that voters feel the economic pain from high gas prices and rising grocery bills in a way that they didn’t two decades ago. “The bottom line is people are experiencing the impact of Trump’s war and other policies,” said Christopher Preble, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington. “Now voters have a chance to register their discontent with how he’s dealing with all this.” POLITICS DRIVING FOREIGN POLICY With Trump’s [USN:L6N465159 TEXT:"approval ratings"] touching historic lows, he has left little doubt, despite his public claims to the contrary, that he sees the straight line voters are drawing between his foreign policy and their cost of living. That has prompted some controversial policy moves in the run-up to the elections. Chief among them was Trump’s lifting of sanctions on [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"Russian diesel"] exports aimed at bringing down fuel prices, a step his critics, including some fellow Republicans, say reinforces the impression that he is increasingly siding with Moscow in its war in Ukraine. He has also pressed Kyiv to halt strikes on [USN:L1N46203J TEXT:"Russian refineries"] as he tries to shift the blame for high US gasoline prices despite experts saying the surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the war he launched alongside Israel against Iran nearly eight months ago. At the same time, he has promised not to order any [USN:FWN45U1SW TEXT:"new attack"] on Iran before the midterms, though the US and Israel are widely reported to be preparing for a possible major escalation after the elections. Polls have shown that most voters oppose the war initiated by Trump, who had campaigned on avoiding new foreign interventions. He has insisted Americans should accept temporarily higher gas prices so that he can block Iran from developing a nuclear weapon. Iran says its nuclear program is for civilian purposes. The UN nuclear watchdog and US intelligence community have assessed that Tehran shuttered a nuclear weapons development program in 2003. Some Republican candidates have [USN:L4N45N1R0 TEXT:"distanced themselves"] from Trump on matters ranging from the conflict in the Middle East to the trade war with Canada and his pressure campaign against Ukraine. For its part, Iran has sought to keep oil prices high and hurt Trump in the midterms by deploying new tactics to target ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz and deliberately prolonging the [USN:L8N46515R TEXT:"diplomatic stalemate"], senior Iranian officials have told Reuters. Defending the administration's approach, White House spokesman Matt Middleton said: "President Trump has always been clear about temporary market disruptions as a result of the conflict in Iran, but the contrast between President Trump’s economic record and Democrats’ ruinous alternative is clear." ‘IT’S THE ECONOMY, STUPID’ Midterm elections historically have been seen as a referendum on the performance of the incumbent in the White House. And in one election after another in recent decades, the conventional wisdom has been that economic concerns - “it’s the economy, stupid,” as the Clinton-era adage goes - dominate voters’ choices. Opinion polls for this year’s midterms, including the Reuters/Ipsos survey, show that while voters rank foreign policy low on their list of priorities, it is clear that most Americans see some of Trump’s signature moves on the world stage, such as the Iran war and tariffs, feeding into their higher costs. Other polls have shown that a majority of Americans have also soured more broadly on Trump’s international approach. The Chicago Council on Global Affairs said its latest nationwide survey “finds that most Americans believe the Trump administration’s foreign policy actions have negatively impacted America’s global standing and hurt national and household economic conditions.” Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has shaken up the rules-based global order that Washington helped create from the ashes of World War Two while his relations with allies have steadily worsened and the [USN:L1N45G0ZJ TEXT:"limits of US power"] have been increasingly exposed, analysts say. LEGISLATIVE BALANCE OF POWER IN PLAY Against this backdrop, Democrats are widely projected to [USN:L6N465159 TEXT:"gain control"] of the House of Representatives in the midterms, with the Senate also seen as increasingly in play. For Republicans, losing either chamber could complicate Trump's agenda in the last two years of his second term. But even with a shift in the balance of power on Capitol Hill on November 3, lawmakers will have a hard time reining in Trump’s capacity to pursue foreign policy as he sees fit. Once the ballots are counted, a big question will be whether Trump will feel either restricted or emboldened on the world stage as he enters what is traditionally considered a lame-duck phase - when a president is barred from running again and no longer faces electoral consequences for decisions made. “For many presidents who feel politically constrained (at home), foreign policy is the area where they are able to act with relative freedom,” said Jon Alterman of the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank in Washington. Analysts say Trump's handling of adversaries such as Iran, Russia, China and even Cuba or his approach to allies across the globe could go either way -- or he could simply lose interest and double down on his string of construction projects, such as the White House ballroom.

item.title: Deni Avdija propels Blazers to comeback victory over Kings
item.description: Deni Avdija scored 26 points and the Portland Trail Blazers overcame a 12-point first-quarter deficit en route to a 128-120 victory over the host Sacramento Kings on Friday night.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Deni Avdija scored 26 points and the Portland Trail Blazers overcame a 12-point first-quarter deficit en route to a 128-120 victory over the host Sacramento Kings on Friday night. Damian Lillard and Toumani Camara scored 19 points apiece and Sidy Cissoko scored 15 points, all in the first half, as Portland improved to 2-0. Robert Williams III scored 13 points while Ja Morant and Jrue Holiday each had 12 points for the Trail Blazers. Kings rookie Darius Acuff Jr. scored 33 points in his second career game and Domantas Sabonis had 27 points, 19 rebounds and 10 assists for his 69th career triple-double. Zach LaVine scored 22 points, Precious Achiuwa added 14 and Keegan Murray had 12 as Sacramento lost its second straight game to open the season. The contest was the Kings' home opener. Portland shot 47.9% from the field, including 14 of 48 (29.2%) from 3-point range. Camara made five 3-pointers and Donovan Clingan grabbed 10 rebounds for the Trail Blazers. The Kings made 46.2% of their attempts and were 8 of 31 (25.8%) from behind the arc. Portland scored the first 15 points of the third quarter to turn a five-point deficit into a 74-64 advantage. Camara scored the final seven points of the burst. Morant drained a 3-pointer to make it 84-73 just prior to the midway point of the quarter. Sacramento trailed 88-83 after Achiuwa's layup with 3:39 remaining in the period before Portland pushed the lead back to 103-90 on Avdija's floater with 1.3 seconds left. The Trail Blazers had an 8-1 edge in 3-pointers during a 44-point third quarter while committing just one turnover. Lillard's short jumper gave Portland a 113-102 edge with 7:09 remaining. Acuff scored the next six points for Sacramento, and he later connected on a 3-pointer to bring the Kings within 118-113 with 4:51 to play. Sacramento got within three, but Camara responded with a trey to give Portland a 121-115 lead with 3:47 left. Four straight points by Clingan gave the Trail Blazers a seven-point lead with 1:50 to play. Avdija sank two free throws to make it an eight-point margin with 28.3 seconds left as Portland sealed its fifth straight victory over the Kings. Sabonis had 17 points, 12 rebounds and seven assists in the first half, when the Kings never trailed. Sacramento led 64-59 at the break. --Field Level Media

item.title: Uncovering 'heat storms'
item.description: Why we needed new language to describe modern heat waves
item.content:encoded:
